items.title: FedEx plane overshoots Miami runway, causing brief suspension of flights at airport
items.summary: The brief ground stop came on the eve of the US Thanksgiving holiday, one of the busiest travel days of the year.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

BySareen Habeshian

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.

Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights are expected to resume by around 22:00 local time, the FAA told the BBC.

The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.

The ground stop comes on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.

Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.

Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.

"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.

The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travelers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.

The Miami-Dade area is under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.

A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

items.body: Having lived and worked in Afghanistan for seven years, photojournalist Élise Blanchard offers an intimate account of what daily life is like for Afghan women today. Joining Genie Godula on the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, she explains how restrictions vary across the country, depending on where women live, their families and the local enforcement of Taliban decrees. She stresses the need to maintain access to healthcare, primary education and food, pointing to severe cuts in humanitarian assistance by the US and EU.

items.title: How Chinese companies circumvent chips sanctions in Southeast Asia
items.summary: High-tech AI chips are hard to get in China because of US restrictions. To get around this, Chinese companies often use offshore computing capacity, particularly in Southeast Asia. The US is also trying to stop it.
items.body:

Some €510 billion ($559 billion) have been invested into AI infrastructure across Malaysia since February 2025. The consulting group Fitch Solutions has opened 125 data centers in Malaysia to serve the global digital economy. The sector is booming in the western Malaysian state of Johor where, according to Malaysia's Digital Ministry, 16 of 27 new data centers are located.

The government in Kuala Lumpur hopes the investment will create numerous new jobs, up to 90% of which are expected to be filled by locals. The advantages of the data center sites include low electricity prices for energy-intensive computing and good links to international submarine cables.

Amazon, Google and Microsoft along Strait of Malacca

Major US technology companies have also set up along the Strait of Malacca. Amazon and Oracle have each invested $6 billion, while Microsoft and Google have invested $2 billion apiece. In early November, Google's parent company, Alphabet, announced additional investments of $15 billion.

"Malaysia's vision is not only to build an economy that uses artificial intelligence, but also one that uses AI creatively,” explained Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo in a statement that was tellingly published in Chinese, which is not an official language of Malaysia.

Trump's ASEAN Play: The new front in the US-China chip war

Data center growth in Southeast Asia is part of the race for technological supremacy in artificial intelligence. The US has restricted the export of high-performance chips, such as those produced by US tech giant Nvidia, to China. It has also tried to block the sale of the advanced lithography machines used to manufacture microchips that are made by Dutch manufacturer ASML.

Chinese companies rent access to US chips

Since Chinese chips have yet to reach the same technological standards as others, some Chinese companies are testing an alternative model in that they legally purchase or lease capacity in other countries. They can thus rent access to US chips that have been installed in systems in Malaysia, for example, and develop their AI models from abroad.

In October, the Institute for Progress (IFP), an independent think tank in Washington, warned that Southeast Asia was becoming an offshore hub for Chinese AI enclaves. It estimated that by the end of the year about 24% of China's total computing power came from remote access to overseas data centers, three-quarters of which were in Southeast Asia. This was predicted to rise to 31% by the end of 2027.

Most of the workers at the data centers in Malaysia are locals Image: Cheng Yiheng/Xinhua/picture alliance

The IFP said that though "US AI chips hosted in overseas data centers are a significant source of compute for China," they were "difficult to size."

It explained that "Chinese entities can rent GPUs [graphics processing units] as a service from cloud providers or lease data center capacity overseas, directly from developers or through intermediaries. Cloud providers and data center developers rarely name their customers or disclose how much capacity each uses, and Chinese companies disclose little themselves."

Alibaba Cloud sets up shop in Malaysia

The Chinese giant Alibaba Cloud currently operates six data centers in Malaysia — three in Johor and three in the greater Kuala Lumpur region, with the most recent one opening on November 19.

The company has invested $53 billion in data centers in total, including in South Korea, Thailand, the Philippines and Mexico, as well as Malaysia. TikTok's parent company also operates data center capacity in Johor.

The race for transformers

In early October, Tencent, another multinational technology conglomerate, which is based in Shenzhen, signed a five-year $7 billion contract with Oracle, allowing it to use computing capacity equivalent to 100,000 modern AI chips for training artificial intelligence. The company was supposed to pay 30% upfront.

The deal fell through a few weeks later, however, and both companies have remained silent about the reasons. According to media reports, there was pressure from the governments in both Beijing and Washington. China wants to develop its own chip industry, whereas high-ranking US officials reportedly raised security concerns with Oracle.

US tariffs on Malaysian imports

In mid-2025, the US threatened to impose an additional 25% tariff on Malaysia imports "to prevent circumvention of export controls on chips," according to the Chinese consulting firm Equal Ocean. "The Malaysian government quickly responded by opposing illegal resale practices and introducing licensing requirements for the transshipment of certain high-end chips."

Washington is now stepping up its efforts. On the same day that US President Donald Trump met with his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China last week, the Bureau of Industry and Security, an agency of the US Department of Commerce, issued new rules with regard to remote access to advanced AI chips and servers.

It said that the goal was "to prevent certain foreign actors from leveraging advanced computing power based on US technology to threaten US national security and foreign policy interests." The restrictions pertain to data centers that provide significant computing capacity to companies with ties to countries in "Country Group D:5 or Macau."

How the China-US AI arms race is escalating

According to US export regulations, the D:5 group includes China, Russia, Iran and North Korea and others. In future, companies will have to conduct more thorough checks to identify the ownership and control structures behind their clients.

Washington has also introduced new licensing requirements for advanced semiconductors destined for Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. Subsidiaries of US companies are exempt.

"The US is not only reviewing which countries will receive AI chips in future but also wants to have a say in where the chips are used, who operates them and which customers they serve," explained Chinese industry expert Xu Sanlang. "This means that data centers, which have been providing remote computing capacity to Chinese clients will have to comply with these restrictions in future."

items.summary: Move comes as US steps up export controls to prevent Chinese access to AI computing power.

Nvidia halts chip shipments to Southeast Asia: Report

Move comes as US steps up export controls to prevent Chinese access to AI computing power.

Nvidia has told its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers to four Southeast Asian countries, as the US steps up export controls to prevent Chinese access to AI computing power.

Manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro, which package Nvidia’s chips into servers, have told buyers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia that Nvidia will not allow their orders to be shipped, according to three people with knowledge of the matter.

It is unclear whether the halt is temporary, as Nvidia and its partners try to work out how to comply with Washington’s new export controls, the people said.

The four Southeast Asian countries have become favoured destinations for Chinese AI developers seeking to access Nvidia’s most advanced chips, whose exports are restricted by Washington.

The region is lucrative for Nvidia. The chipmaker booked US$104 billion of revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025, a 72 per cent increase in 12 months, according to company accounts. Nvidia also records some of its Taiwan and China revenue via its Singapore unit.

Many Chinese groups get around US export controls by renting access through cloud computing providers that buy servers containing Nvidia chips.

Jensen Huang’s stunning return as Nvidia CEO: A timeline of events

US chip export curbs test Southeast Asia’s AI ambitions, but offer chance to toughen regulatory oversight

The US commerce department introduced new rules last week aimed at stopping the practice. The measures came after Jensen Huang was briefly ousted as chief executive of Nvidia following reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman tied to a cloud provider that leased access to Chinese companies and is being investigated for alleged involvement in smuggling.

The revelations complicated Huang’s stance that the US should continue selling Nvidia chips to Chinese companies to increase their dependence on American technology.

Despite Beijing’s push to develop domestic alternatives, China’s leading AI labs remain heavily reliant on Nvidia’s processors to develop their flagship models, particularly during compute-intensive early-stage training.

While many were hoping Huang’s return to the helm of Nvidia this week would open a path to less strict enforcement of the new rules, there is little indication that the company will hold back from executing them, said the people.

The commerce department has set a 90-day deadline for cloud providers to obtain a licence by proving that their end users do not include restricted entities.

“There’s this new rule but no guidance on execution,” said an executive at a cloud provider. “No one knows how to apply for this licence while the 90-day clock is ticking. It’s causing sheer chaos in the region.”

Demand from Chinese tech companies has fuelled Southeast Asia’s data centre boom, particularly in Malaysia and Indonesia, where billions of dollars have poured into the construction of AI infrastructure. The new US restrictions have put much of that investment in jeopardy.

Among those affected is Aolani, a Singapore-based cloud company that planned to provide advanced computing power to ByteDance, the Chinese owner of TikTok, through leasing agreements, said two of the people.

The disruption has led some bankers who previously agreed to finance the project to stop issuing credit worth about $500mn and to ByteDance potentially dropping the deal.

Nvidia declined to comment. Dell, Supermicro, ByteDance and Aolani did not respond to requests for comment.

This story was first published in The Financial Times.

items.title: Can Rassvet, 'Russia's Starlink' change the course of the war in Ukraine?
items.summary: SpaceX's US Starlink satellite system has played a key role in countering the Russian military in Ukraine, but now a Russian counterpart is under development. What could this mean for Ukraine in future?
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PtKd

Prefer DW on Google

Electronic warfare is an important component in Russia's war against Ukraine Image: Alexander Polegenko/picture alliance

Advertisement

Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX. Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit. Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.

Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's dependence on satellites

What is Rassvet?

Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026. According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks. The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.

HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."

Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.

According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory. He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.

Starlink terminals are used by both the Russian and Ukrainian armies for communications Image: Lev Radin/picture alliance

SpaceX remains far superior to Rassvet in tech terms

Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."

"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company. He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."

"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."

SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors. According to DW's sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink. Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.

But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos. In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.

Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?

Did SpaceX throttle Starlink in Ukraine?

Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine. "Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.

Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.

Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX. Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit. Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine. On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.
Starlink disruption exposes Ukraine's dependence on satellites
What is Rassvet?

Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026. According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks. The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.
HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."

Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."

"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company. He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."

In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.

Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. items.title: S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch
items.summary: S&P said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects.

Business

S&P warns Nvidia's board may be compromised, puts chipmaker's rating on downgrade watch

S&P said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects.

File photo. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang speaks with Alice Huang after delivering a keynote speech at COMPUTEX 2024 in Taipei, Taiwan, Jun 2, 2024. (Photo: Reuters/Ann Wang)

S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia's credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade on Wednesday (Nov 25), saying the departure and subsequent reinstatement of its CEO had exposed weaknesses in the chipmaker's management and board oversight.

"We believe the long tenure of certain board members may have compromised their independence. The company's corporate governance practices may also not have kept pace with Nvidia's rapid growth and its role as a critical global technology enabler," the ratings agency said.

The move comes amid a turbulent period for Nvidia's leadership. The company's board reinstated CEO Jensen Huang earlier this week, days after he resigned following revelations of extramarital affairs with his direct reports as well as a Chinese businesswoman alleged by US intelligence to be Beijing's spy.

Critics and lawmakers slammed the reinstatement, questioning the independence of the board, whose newly elected chair had told investors last week Nvidia would not rehire Huang as CEO because his personal behaviour was inconsistent with the company's code of conduct.

Reinstating Huang on Monday, Nvidia omitted any mention of his affairs, saying instead the move was "based on US government input", even as an independent board committee continued its investigation into reports involving him and a suspected foreign intelligence effort.

Reuters reported on Wednesday that the US Justice Department did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before US President Donald Trump pushed for his return as CEO, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Instead, it concluded that there was no evidence he had broken any laws based on ongoing investigations into two Nvidia clients, Super Micro and Megaspeed International, which are suspected of smuggling advanced microchips to China. That determination is subject to change as the probes continue.

Jensen Huang’s stunning return as Nvidia CEO: A timeline of events

Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

NO EVIDENCE YET THAT ALICE HUANG IS A SPY

Investors were largely unruffled by the S&P move, which comes with Nvidia shares down 38 per cent since Oct 6. Nvidia closed down nearly 4 per cent on Wednesday, retracing some declines after the Nasdaq 100 index briefly flirted with a 20 per cent decline from its recent high.

The cost of insurance against tech companies defaulting on debts has jumped sharply in recent weeks, but the five-year CDS spread for Nvidia was little changed.

Nvidia currently has an AA rating from S&P, which indicates a very strong capacity to meet financial commitments. The highest rating is AAA.

The agency said it could downgrade Nvidia within the next 90 days, but expects any potential downgrade to be limited to one notch, unless investigations and other disclosures harm the company's reputation or future business prospects.

Meanwhile, Moody's said on Wednesday that bringing back Huang eases near-term uncertainty around Nvidia's business execution and eliminates execution risk associated with appointing a new leader for the chipmaker.

The agency said Nvidia's Aa1 rating and stable outlook remain unaffected, but added that governance and regulatory uncertainty persists.

Nvidia has played a key role in financing the AI boom, bankrolling AI startups, cloud firms and data-center projects, which in turn spend much of that capital on Nvidia's own GPUs and other AI chips.

The complex financing arrangements have increased Nvidia's exposure to a potential downturn, analysts said.

Separately, the Wall Street Journal on Wednesday reported that US officials found no evidence that tech executive Alice Huang was directed by Beijing to spy on Jensen Huang, citing people familiar with a classified briefing.

Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and National Security Agency briefed staff from congressional intelligence committees and chamber leaders, the Journal reported.

The officials said Alice Huang contacted China's spy agency during the affair but found no indication that she provided significant intelligence, the Journal reported.

Nvidia and the agencies did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. Reuters could not independently verify the report.

The report said current evidence suggests Alice Huang and Jensen Huang may have had an amorous relationship, but it was not a coordinated play by China, and that new information could change that assessment.

The briefing also noted that Kang Wei, described to the Journal as Alice Huang's husband by people who know them, was an asset for China's Ministry of State Security who remained in frequent contact with the intelligence service.

Source: Reuters/aj

Trump and NATO chief urge Russia to avoid actions that widen Ukraine war

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte speaks to the media on the day of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting at NATO headquarters in Brussels, Belgium, on Nov 17, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Stephanie Lecocq)

WASHINGTON: Russia should avoid actions that expand its war in Ukraine, US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte said in a joint statement on Wednesday (Nov 26) after a meeting in Florida where they also discussed the Iran war.

The meeting came after the Republican leader, who has been critical of America's Western ⁠allies, met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last week in Asia, referring to each as his "friend."

"We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," the leaders said in their statement.

Trump's meeting with ​Putin triggered a backlash from domestic Democratic opponents and European allies, with the latter having ‌pushed ⁠to be included in US-backed talks to end the war in Ukraine.

Elon Musk, the world's richest person, said on Wednesday (Nov 25) that every child in the US will receive two shares in SpaceX, the space and AI company he runs, pledging a gift worth some US$18 billion.

Musk and rival AI company Anthropic have recently laid out sharply different blueprints for sharing some of the spoils of the AI boom, amid growing public and political scrutiny of the industry.

Children will receive one share from the company and one from him personally, Musk said in a brief post on X, without providing details.

In a separate post, Musk said the SpaceX shares will be transferred next month.

"The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," Musk added.

SpaceX said earlier on Wednesday it would contribute one newly issued share of its Class A common stock to every currently active Trump Account, adding that Musk will personally match the number of shares donated by the company.

A Trump Account is a program designed to give Americans under the age of 18 a stake in the stock market and help build wealth from an early age. The White House said in October it had opened almost 70 million accounts. SpaceX shares closed at US$127.44 on Wednesday, valuing the pledge at nearly US$18 billion.

SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Musk's SpaceX share donations would be linked to Trump Accounts.

"What it does is build a massive, long-term retail shareholder base," said Christopher Brankin, global markets advisor at brokerage Mitrade Group. "It builds immediate market engagement and creates a massive, financially literate client pipeline for trading platforms as that generation comes of age."

Musk, whose net worth is around US$824 billion, said last month he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America. He held about 6.42 billion shares in the company as of June.

"Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X at the time.

"Giving shares, which are stakes in the future economy, directly to the people is the way," Musk added.

Most of Musk's philanthropic efforts have been through the Musk Foundation, which reportedly holds more than US$14 billion in assets.

In October, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell and her husband pledged a share of their SpaceX stock to each of more than 2 million children under the Trump initiative.

Anthropic, which recently went public, said last month it was committing 5 per cent of its shares to a new fund for the "public good".

It said that the initiative, worth around US$54 billion at current prices, will give it more flexibility and scale to make donations for the benefit of humanity.

Other executives have also set up major, long-running philanthropy ventures.

Berkshire Hathaway Chairman Emeritus Warren Buffett, one of the most prominent figures in philanthropy, is reported to have given away US$60 billion so far, with most of the rest of his roughly US$150 billion fortune slated for philanthropy too.

The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation has distributed more than US$100 billion since its founding in 2000, with some of that fueled by donations from Buffett.

ByJonathan Josephs and Osmond Chia, Business reporters

The US is preparing to announce plans for new tariffs on several countries as early as Wednesday, the BBC understands.

The new import taxes would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, with China, the European Union and Japan among at least 14 jurisdictions affected.

The move comes after the White House's so-called "Section 301" investigation. It was launched in March after the US Supreme Court ruled that President Donald Trump's Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.

Trump has made tariffs a signature policy of his presidency, arguing that they will help boost American manufacturing and create jobs.

The president sent shockwaves around the world when he unveiled sweeping tariffs on global trading partners in April 2025 shortly after his return to the White House.

While the tariffs were later struck down, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer argued then that overproduction abroad was displacing American manufacturing and deterring investment.

Under the new tariffs, countries will face different import tax rates depending on the deals that they have previously struck with Trump.

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, which remain locked in a trade dispute.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and President Xi Jinping, the two sides have yet to fully resolve their difference with an interim agreement set to expire on 10 January.

In the run up to the Shenzhen summit, the US accused China of not fully living up to the terms of what it agreed in October 2025.

However earlier on Tuesday China extended the suspension of a ban on exports critical minerals including gallium, germanium, antimony until 27 January. The ban would otherwise have come into force on Friday.

Commentary: New US tariff threat seeks to ramp up pressure on trading partners – will it work?

This strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, says Steven Okun from APAC Advisors.

A 3D-printed miniature model depicting U.S. President Donald Trump depicting U.S. flag and word "Tariffs" in this illustration taken, April 17, 2025. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration

SINGAPORE: The Trump administration sticks with its America First trade agenda after a shellacking in the US midterms by firing its latest trade salvo on 14 major trading partners, including China, Japan, the European Union and several Southeast Asian countries such as Singapore, Malaysia and Vietnam.

Singapore could be among the hardest hit despite having a free trade agreement (FTA) and running a trade deficit with the US. Under the proposed duties aimed at what Washington terms as excess industrial capacity, Singapore faces a principal tariff rate of up to 20 per cent from the US.

The latest raft of tariffs, announced on Wednesday (Nov 25) and are not due to kick in until January after a period of consultation, ranged from headline rates of 20 per cent to 40 per cent.

But the US Trade Representative (USTR) has given other governments an out with potential lower rates – if they enter or already have an agreement with the US.

This means those with an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (ART) are not impacted – so long as the agreement remains in force. The European Commission, for instance, said in a statement that it expects any measures imposed by the US to respect the 15 per cent ceiling agreed last year, while rejecting US’ claim that Europe is a source of structural overcapacity.

The proposed tariffs are therefore aimed at pushing those which do not have an ART, such as India, Vietnam and Singapore, to sign one.

Singapore 'very disappointed' with proposed US tariffs, says findings fail to account for its economic structure

Asian governments push back, seek deals after Trump’s new tariff salvo

For example, Vietnam faces a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if it reaches a trade agreement with the US, rising to 35 per cent if negotiations fail. Washington trade insiders expect the Southeast Asian country to sign one on the sidelines of the coming G20 meeting in Miami next month.

India, which remains in talks with the US on a trade deal, would see a 17 per cent tariff rate if an agreement is finalised and a 25 per cent rate if talks fail.

For Singapore, it is 10 per cent with an agreement and 20 per cent without one.

SINGAPORE COULD BE THE HARDEST HIT

Among the 14 trading partners slapped with new tariffs, Singapore stands out as one which has yet to negotiate a trade deal with the US. A 20 per cent rate would also match the Southeast Asian region’s highest rate, presuming Vietnam enters its own ART and similar deals inked by other regional countries remain in force.

“Despite the bilateral FTA and a US trade surplus with Singapore, the Trump administration seems to believe it can extract more and apparently sees little downside risk in trying,” Barbara Weisel of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace told me.

Commentary: Trump’s tariff wall isn’t going anywhere

Snap Insight: US midterms – what an angry ‘lame duck’ president could mean for Asia

There may be other reasons for the USTR’s desire to get Singapore to the negotiating table.

At a recent economic conference organised by the American Chamber of Commerce in Singapore, US Ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha said that President Donald Trump requires him to “bring some money” back to the US by increasing Singaporean investment.

Singapore’s foreign direct investment in the United States stands at roughly US$72 billion, making it the third largest in Asia, based on the US Department of Commerce’s data as of 2024. Ambassador Sinha said he expects that number to double.

One will expect the US to require Singapore to announce an increase in FDI if a negotiation happens, as it has done with others.

Singapore has previously said it is taking a cautious approach to any concessions that could secure a lower tariff from the US. In a parliamentary reply in August, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said the Singapore government must first assess the significant costs and wider trade implications of measures sought by Washington.

It has also persistently denied that its exports to the world’s largest economy are due to some form of excess capacity.

The country's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry on Thursday morning said it disagrees with the USTR's findings.

WEIGHING THE OPTIONS

Trading partners that do not yet have an ART will have to weigh the actual impact of these potentially higher tariffs versus what they will be required to concede.

Beyond increases in investment commitments, another factor will be what other requirements the US would include, which could relate to trade with China such as those reported to be included in the US negotiations with Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam.

For example, Malaysia agreed to closer cooperation with Washington on export controls, investment screening, transshipment, critical minerals and sensitive technologies – all of which could impact its relations with China. China’s Ministry of Commerce noted last year it had “ serious concerns” regarding parts of the Malaysia-US agreement.

Another ironic twist of these tariffs finds the Trump administration calling foreign governments “unreasonable and unfair” for having their own industrial plans and promoting that their own citizens save money.

An example of the latter is the USTR's mention of Singapore's Central Provident Fund as a policy it deems unreasonable. It had noted that a requirement for citizens to contribute “upwards of 20 per cent of their income” to the programme exceeds that of the US and many developed economies, and that it “promotes savings in a way that depresses consumption”.

In other words, it places tariffs on external governments such as Singapore, for putting their people first.

TARIFFS MAY HAVE A SHORT SHELF-LIFE

The latest trade salvo comes despite US voters making their unhappiness known with the administration’s approach to trade. This should be no surprise though, as Mr Trump's decades-long belief in tariffs will never change.

But the courts have found that the administration often exceeds its authority in issuing them. In February, the US Supreme Court struck down Mr Trump’s so-called “Liberation Day” tariffs. That may again happen here.

The US’ strategy of forcing trading partners to the negotiating table may not work as it once did, given the legal defeats and the likelihood these tariffs may not outlast the administration anyway.

Governments will have to weigh whether to accept a proposed higher rate of tariff under the latest round of “Section 301” probe, which may not last that long, rather than giving up concessions on investment and China-related commitments.

With legal decisions looming and the back half of Trump 2.0 about to start, governments may also reassess how much leverage the US still has.

Steven Okun serves as CEO of APAC Advisors, a geostrategic and responsible investment consultancy based in Singapore. He served as Deputy General Counsel at the US Department of Transportation in the Administration of President Bill Clinton.

items.title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to severe weather
items.summary: The was the first time ever that the iconic celebration was delayed because of storms. New York expects damaging winds and heavy rainfall over the Thanksgiving holiday.
items.body:
Figure caption,

New York City mayor on postponing 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade

ByNardine Saad

Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.

Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.

The last time the parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.

A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.

Image source, Getty Images

The potent nor'easter storm is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.

Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.

"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.

Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.

Macy's confirmed the new parade date and updated a countdown clock on its website to reflect the Saturday schedule. Meanwhile, broadcaster NBC has said it will show the 2025 parade on Thursday.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who will not attend the parade on Saturday because of a scheduled surgery, said at the news conference that "you have to plan for every possibility" and confirmed that "extreme weather has forced" officials to make the change.

"We know that this is an inconvenience for many who come to visit our city. This decision, however, was made with safety being paramount," he said. "We want to ensure that we're delivering a parade that's not only incredible and spectacular, but one also that doesn't come at the expense of anyone's safety."

Mamdani also said that there would be an expanded police presence along the parade route on Saturday and that there were "no known specific or credible threats to the parade at this time".

Cross added that Macy's is working through what costs it could cover as a result of the delay and said the company is in contact with bands, performers and others who travelled to the city for the parade.

Figure caption,

BBC Weather's Elizabeth Rizzini looks at the weather that will impact travel over US Thanksgiving.

During some past parades, strong winds and inclement weather have led to the tearing and deflation of the balloons as well as collisions with lampposts that caused injuries.

The US National Weather Service has issued a high wind warning, valid from 10:00 local time (15:00 GMT) on Thursday until 01:00 (06:00 GMT) on Friday with gusts potentially reaching 60mph (97km/h) - although the very strongest winds are likely to occur after the parade was due to end.

Heavy rain and coastal flooding will pose additional hazards across the eastern US as the storm sweeps through, while some inland parts could also see snow, BBC Weather reports.

The governor of the neighbouring state of New Jersey on Wednesday declared a state of emergency across the state's 21 counties, beginning at 18:00 local time (23:00 GMT).

Governor Mikie Sherrill's office said the powerful coastal storm is expected to bring damaging winds, heavy rainfall, and severe tidal flooding through Friday, with coastal and bayside communities facing the greatest risk. Sherrill urged residents to stay off the roads as much as possible once the storm arrives.

Image source, EPA

Image caption,

The balloons will be deflated again and then re-inflated for Saturday

Originally called the Macy's Christmas Parade, the celebration, which also features live performers, debuted in 1924 as a way to boost holiday sales. It was founded by Macy's employees and their families.

From 1942 to 1944 New York went without the parade as the US directed materials like rubber and helium toward the country's war effort.

The 2.5mi (4km) procession route begins at Macy's Herald Square flagship store and concludes in Manhattan's Upper West Side, with performers and spectators lining the streets to greet Santa Claus and ring in the holiday season.

Country artist Megan Moroney and Grammy nominee Teddy Swims were slated to perform at the flagship store, but it is unclear whether they, along with the dozens of celebrities and float performers on the roster, would be returning on Saturday.

items.title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
items.summary: Somalia relies heavily on foreign funding and military support for its very survival.
items.body:
Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external support

ByBasillioh Rukanga

Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.

The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.

Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.

The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.

The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.

Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.

Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.

The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.

With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.

The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.

Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.

He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.

"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.

The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.

Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.

• Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia?Published15 March 2012

Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.

In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.

His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.

Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.

They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.

Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.

But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.

He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.

Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.

He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.

He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.

"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.

During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.

Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007

Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.

Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.

He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.

It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.

But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.

Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.

This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says.

The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.

The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.

Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.

Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.

Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.

But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.

The dispute escalated this year after Mohamud pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.

Image source, AFP via Getty Images

Image caption,

Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the government

This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.

A day before the ruling, Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. He and other judges in the case have filed a suit against Somalia over the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.

The Somali government has since rejected the Supreme Court's decision, with its implementation now uncertain.

Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.

Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government.

"Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he said.

He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.

Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?

Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.

Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.

Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid.

Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.

But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.

He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.

That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.

Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images

Image caption,

Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign support

Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.

The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.

The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.

The dispute illustrates the difficult relationship Somalia has with foreign partners on whom it relies for security, funding and political support.

For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.

He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.

But Guleid remains far less optimistic.

He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made.

For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave.

Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.

New Miss Universe’s Puerto Rican hometown celebrates her historic win as first mother and first married woman to take title

Jennifer Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work.

Puerto Rico's Jennifer Barreto, Miss Universe 2026, attends a press conference after the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Wednesday, Nov 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Alejandro Granadillo)

FAST

The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers”.

Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday (Nov 24) as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe.

“It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement.

The town of some 39,000 people – named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers – could barely contain itself.

“La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win.

“So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.”

Miss Puerto Rico's Jennifer Barreto reacts after winning the Miss Universe at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Alejandro Granadillo)

Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the US Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviours.

“Her journey is a powerful reminder that motherhood, marriage and personal ambition are not mutually exclusive, and that a woman’s potential should never be defined by the stage of life she is in,” Ronald Day, CEO of the Miss Universe Organization, said in a statement.

The organisation began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023. The pageant has lost favour in some countries, with critics saying it objectifies women and promotes unrealistic body ideals.

Barreto is the sixth Puerto Rican woman to win the Miss Universe crown, ending a 20-year wait for the island.

“I am ready to go to work,” she said at a news conference after the contest, which she called “the Olympics of beauty.”

“You know that I am a highly disciplined woman,” Barreto said, adding that she likes challenges. “I aspire to earn the affection and respect of you all.”

Her hometown became known for “Pepino Power”, a volunteer brigade formed to restore electricity after Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in 2017 as a Category 4 storm.

Puerto Rico now has the third-most Miss Universe titles, behind the United States with nine and Venezuela with seven.

Celebrating Barreto's win was Yazaira Cabrera, a 50-year-old gymnastics coach who loves beauty pageants so much that she had a replica crown made based on the one worn by Puerto Rican Miss Universe 2021 Denise Quiñones.

Cabrera wore it Tuesday night as she watched the contest at home, feeling nervous the entire time.

“They kept us on edge until the very end,” she said. “The whole country was holding its breath.”

Barreto was greeted by thunderous applause at Puerto Rico’s José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum each time she advanced through the competition’s final rounds.

She brought her hands to her face in shock as she was named Miss Universe 2026, beating Miss Dominican Republic and Miss Venezuela. Minutes later, she shimmied in celebration to ABBA’s Dancing Queen.

And thousands of Puerto Ricans across the US territory danced with her.

“It’s a truly spectacular achievement,” San Sebastián Mayor Eladio Cardona Quiles told The Associated Press. “All the most beautiful women in the universe are there, and she managed to stand out. I’m happy she represented ‘los pepinianos.’”

Cardona attended the pageant, while fans gathered in San Sebastián’s public plaza to watch on a big screen. Afterward, they formed a caravan, honking their horns into the night to celebrate Barreto’s victory.

The new Miss Universe hails from a Puerto Rican town whose residents have long been known as “the cucumbers”.

Nestled in the mountains of western Puerto Rico, San Sebastián has been celebrating since Jennifer Barreto made history late Tuesday (Nov 24) as the first mother and first married woman to win Miss Universe.
“It was a day for the history books!” exclaimed one municipal worker at the mayor’s office, which was abuzz with excitement.
The town of some 39,000 people – named after its famous karst formations that look like cucumbers – could barely contain itself.
“La Barreto,” as she’s known, was on the lips of many across San Sebastián hours after the win.
“So excited!” said María Rivera as she juggled orders Wednesday morning at El Guayabal bakery. “We were sure she was going to win.”
Miss Puerto Rico's Jennifer Barreto reacts after winning the Miss Universe at the 75th Miss Universe pageant in San Juan, Puerto Rico, Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026. (AP Photo/Alejandro Granadillo)

Barreto, 27, has one daughter and two master’s degrees, in research psychology and clinical social work. She also works as a prevention specialist with the US Department of Defense, developing strategies to combat harmful behaviours.

“Her journey is a powerful reminder that motherhood, marriage and personal ambition are not mutually exclusive, and that a woman’s potential should never be defined by the stage of life she is in,” Ronald Day, CEO of the Miss Universe Organization, said in a statement.

The organisation began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023. The pageant has lost favour in some countries, with critics saying it objectifies women and promotes unrealistic body ideals.
Barreto is the sixth Puerto Rican woman to win the Miss Universe crown, ending a 20-year wait for the island.
“I am ready to go to work,” she said at a news conference after the contest, which she called “the Olympics of beauty.”
“You know that I am a highly disciplined woman,” Barreto said, adding that she likes challenges. “I aspire to earn the affection and respect of you all.”
Her hometown became known for “Pepino Power”, a volunteer brigade formed to restore electricity after Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in 2017 as a Category 4 storm.
Puerto Rico now has the third-most Miss Universe titles, behind the United States with nine and Venezuela with seven.

Celebrating Barreto's win was Yazaira Cabrera, a 50-year-old gymnastics coach who loves beauty pageants so much that she had a replica crown made based on the one worn by Puerto Rican Miss Universe 2021 Denise Quiñones.
Cabrera wore it Tuesday night as she watched the contest at home, feeling nervous the entire time.
“They kept us on edge until the very end,” she said. “The whole country was holding its breath.”
Barreto was greeted by thunderous applause at Puerto Rico’s José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum each time she advanced through the competition’s final rounds.
She brought her hands to her face in shock as she was named Miss Universe 2026, beating Miss Dominican Republic and Miss Venezuela. Minutes later, she shimmied in celebration to ABBA’s Dancing Queen.
And thousands of Puerto Ricans across the US territory danced with her.

“It’s a truly spectacular achievement,” San Sebastián Mayor Eladio Cardona Quiles told The Associated Press. “All the most beautiful women in the universe are there, and she managed to stand out. I’m happy she represented ‘los pepinianos.’”

Cardona attended the pageant, while fans gathered in San Sebastián’s public plaza to watch on a big screen. Afterward, they formed a caravan, honking their horns into the night to celebrate Barreto’s victory.

SINGAPORE: Asian trading partners pushed back against US President Donald Trump’s latest tariff salvo on Thursday (Nov 26), with Singapore saying it was “very disappointed” by the proposed duties and Japan calling the move “regrettable”.

South Korea said it would hold further talks with Washington to safeguard its interests, while Vietnam sought to quickly conclude a trade deal and Taiwan expressed confidence its previously agreed 15 per cent tariff rate would hold.

China and India have also rejected Washington’s claims over excess industrial capacity.

The responses came after the Trump administration proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including some of Asia’s biggest economies and manufacturing hubs.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) proposed headline tariff rates of between 20 per cent and 40 per cent to counter what Washington described as excess industrial capacity and other market-distorting practices that undermine US manufacturing.

But the actual duties could be capped at lower rates under trade agreements already concluded or still being negotiated with Washington.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the tariffs would not take effect until after a Jan 25 public hearing.

SINGAPORE "VERY DISAPPOINTED"

Singapore said it disagreed with the USTR’s findings and was “very disappointed” with the proposed actions.

The Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry (METI) said the findings did not take into account the structure of Singapore’s outward- and market-oriented economy.

“Singapore’s economic policies do not protect our domestic market or subsidise manufacturing for export,” the ministry said.

METI said it had actively engaged the USTR throughout the investigation and “thoroughly addressed its queries and concerns”.

Singapore will submit further comments during the upcoming public consultation period and continue engaging Washington, including urging the USTR to reconsider its proposed measures and exploring ways to reduce the tariff.

The USTR has proposed tariffs of up to 20 per cent on Singapore goods, with exemptions for certain products.

CHINA REJECTS "OVERCAPACITY" AS POLITICAL PRETEXT

China rejected Washington’s allegation that it was a source of excess industrial capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” a spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington said.

The spokesperson urged both sides to jointly deliver on agreements reached between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Under the excess factory capacity probe, USTR said China would face the highest capped rate of 20 per cent, which would be added to duties of roughly 25 per cent imposed during Trump's first term.

That rate would comply with a US-China trade truce that expires on Jan 10. But if the truce unravels, China's rate would rise to 40 per cent, the USTR said.

JAPAN CALLS TARIFF PROPOSAL ‘REGRETTABLE’

Japan on Thursday called Washington’s proposed tariffs “regrettable” and rejected the US assertion that it had structural excess manufacturing capacity.

"Japan does not have any non-market policy practices or structural excess production capacity," said Japan's top government spokesman Minoru Kihara.

"It is regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced in spite of this."

Trump announces new tariffs on 14 trading partners including China and Singapore

VIETNAM PUSHES FOR TRADE DEAL

Vietnam said it was working to finalise a trade deal with the United States, vowed to act on "overcapacity" and to tighten forced labour regulations in an effort to avoid Washington's proposed new tariffs.

The ministry said it would participate fully in the next stages of the USTR investigation, including registering for and attending the public hearing, presenting its views and responding to questions from US officials.

The US is Vietnam's largest export market; the US' trade deficit with Vietnam is the largest that it has with any partner.

Vietnam has yet to conclude its trade negotiations with Washington.

Under the USTR proposal, Vietnamese goods would face a capped tariff rate of 20 per cent if an agreement is reached. The rate could rise to 35 per cent if negotiations fail.

Vietnam said it had made commitments under a framework trade agreement in October 2025 and made reforms to address US concerns.

"At the same time, efforts will be made to prevent the risk of overcapacity, curb illegal circumvention and transshipment, combat origin fraud, and effectively enforce regulations prohibiting the import of goods produced using forced labour," it said.

Vietnam and the US meanwhile "are working toward finalising negotiations for a reciprocal, fair, and balanced trade agreement as soon as possible".

Taken together, "these factors will serve as a crucial basis for the United States to consider applying a tariff rate lower than the maximum level proposed in the preliminary findings".

INDIA REJECTS EXCESS CAPACITY CLAIM

India said on Wednesday it was examining the USTR notice and reiterated that it did not have structural excess capacity in any sector.

New Delhi said it had engaged constructively throughout the US investigation and argued that trade-related concerns should be addressed through its ongoing negotiations with Washington for a bilateral trade agreement.

“India remains committed to working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion” of the agreement, its trade ministry said.

Under the latest US proposal, Indian imports would face tariffs of up to 25 per cent, but Greer said the rate would be capped at 17 per cent if the two sides strike a trade deal.

New Delhi and Washington agreed to a framework for a trade deal in February, which brought down a punitive tariff on most Indian goods from 50 per cent to 18 per cent. The higher rate had been imposed in August 2025 after an earlier round of negotiations collapsed.

Subsequently, the Supreme Court invalidated Trump's use of emergency powers to impose sweeping tariffs globally, leading to a 10 per cent baseline rate.

But a final trade deal between two of the world's biggest economies remains elusive.

Washington has cited India’s industrial expansion policies, inadequate labour protections, market access barriers and failure to address global excess capacity among practices it says disadvantage US producers.

TAIWAN CONFIDENT 15% RATE WILL HOLD

Taiwan said it was confident Washington would maintain the 15 per cent tariff rate previously agreed between the two sides.

Taiwan and the US signed an investment cooperation memorandum of understanding in January and an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade in February.

Those arrangements secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other technology products, which account for more than 70 per cent of Taiwan's exports to the US.

Based on communications between Taipei and Washington, Taiwan's government said it is confident that both sides will maintain the previously agreed-upon 15 per cent.

"The US has one main goal, which is to rebuild the legal basis for its reciprocal tariff policy. It is not to change the content of the agreements themselves," Taiwan Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun, who has led trade talks with Washington, told reporters.

"Both sides have repeatedly said they hope to maintain the content of the agreements. So the agreement as a whole will not change and will not be renegotiated," she added.

Separate Section 232 tariffs on semiconductors and their derivatives have not yet been announced, but Taiwan has already secured most-favoured treatment in advance through the MOU, Cheng said.

Taiwan is home to TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, which is investing US$265 billion to build new factories in the US.

Under January's deal with the US, Taiwanese companies will invest US$250 billion to boost production of semiconductors, energy and artificial intelligence in the US, while Taiwan will also guarantee an additional US$250 billion in credit to facilitate further investment.

Taiwan is also investing US$4.4 billion in a new liquefied natural gas project in Alaska that Trump has championed, though details remain to be ironed out.

Commentary: Trump’s tariff wall isn’t going anywhere

Commentary: Middle powers need the US – when it comes to China exports

SOUTH KOREA SEEKS FURTHER TALKS

South Korea said it would hold further consultations with Washington to safeguard its national interests, while arguing that its manufacturing sector was an integral part of US supply chains.

Seoul’s Industry Ministry said it had stressed during consultations before the announcement that the issue of excess industrial capacity did not apply to South Korea.

The USTR proposed a capped tariff rate of 15 per cent on South Korean goods, including existing most-favoured-nation duties.

However, the rate could rise to 25 per cent depending on the outcome of follow-up consultations and progress in implementing existing trade agreements.

South Korea and the US reached a trade agreement last year to lower tariffs on South Korean exports from 25 per cent in exchange for a combined US$350 billion investment package.

THAILAND SAYS RATE IN LINE WITH EARLIER TALKS

Thailand said Washington’s proposed tariff of up to 18 per cent on Thai goods was in line with previous negotiations between the two sides.

The commerce ministry said the proposed rate would help Thai products remain competitive in the US, Thailand’s biggest export market.
